articles.summary: Iranian state television has warned that modified versions of its Khorramshahr ballistic missile could potentially reach US military installations in
articles.body: Iranian state television has warned that modified versions of its Khorramshahr ballistic missile could potentially reach US military installations in Europe, specifically naming RAF Fairford in Britain, as Tehran continues to issue threats against American targets amid escalating tensions in West Asia. The warning comes alongside claims of Iranian drone strikes targeting a US military radar installation in Bahrain and security alerts issued by Saudi Arabia.According to Iran International, a report broadcast on Iranian state television on Saturday said modifications to the Khorramshahr missile's warhead could significantly extend its range, potentially placing American military bases farther from Iran within reach. "The range of Iran's missiles is not limited to what they have seen," the broadcast said, while suggesting that British air defences might not be more effective than Israel's at intercepting Iranian missiles.The Khorramshahr-4, unveiled in 2023, has a claimed range of 2,000 kilometres and can carry a 1,500-kg warhead. A lighter warhead could theoretically increase its range, although there is no independent confirmation that Iran has developed a modified version capable of reaching Britain.Iran warns US against further escalationThe broadcast also referred to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's October 31 directive instructing the armed forces to retaliate against American and Israeli attacks without geographical restrictions. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) subsequently indicated that Iran's longstanding self-imposed 2,000-km limit on ballistic missile ranges had been lifted.Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Baqer Qalibaf warned Washington against further escalation, saying Tehran would not remain trapped in a situation of "neither war nor peace".Addressing lawmakers on Sunday, Qalibaf said Iran was open to negotiations if Washington accepted its seven conditions. "We do not care whether the US chooses the path of negotiations or war. If it accepts our seven reasonable conditions, the door to an agreement will be open," he said, according to Mehr.On the military front, the IRGC claimed that six drones had struck a US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain. Bahrain's Interior Ministry subsequently issued two security alerts warning residents about potential hazards. Separately, a report by The Wall Street Journal, citing US intelligence officials, estimated that Iran could still possess between 1,500 and 2,500 missiles despite months of American and Israeli strikes.Strait of Hormuz emerges as another flashpointTensions have also intensified around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian naval forces claimed that three oil tankers had caught fire after striking naval mines.According to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC Navy said two tankers attempting to cross the waterway without authorisation had exploded after hitting mines while allegedly operating with their tracking and identification systems switched off.Iran's Armed Forces Navy separately reported that another tanker had caught fire east of the strait after entering what it described as a prohibited maritime zone despite earlier warnings.The Iranian Navy warned that other vessels entering the restricted area could face similar consequences, further raising concerns over maritime security and the disruption of shipping through one of the world's most strategically important energy corridors.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cape Verde votes in election that could deliver first woman president
articles.summary: Cape Verde voted on Sunday in a presidential election that could see the island nation elect its first woman head of state since independence from
articles.body: Cape Verde voted on Sunday in a presidential election that could see the island nation elect its first woman head of state since independence from Portugal in 1975.Incumbent Jose Maria Neves is seeking a second term against former justice minister Joana Rosa, whose campaign has focused on the need for political balance and better opportunities for young people.The election comes as the West African archipelago grapples with a steady exodus of young people seeking work abroad. With a population of around 500,000, Cape Verde has a larger diaspora overseas, particularly in the United States and Portugal.Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans living abroad are registered to vote, accounting for almost a fifth of the electorate.Neves, who served as prime minister for 15 years before becoming president in 2021, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages. He has also promised to organise a youth summit during a second term.Rosa, the candidate of the opposition Movement for Democracy (MpD), has called for policies that allow young people to build their futures at home rather than leave the country. She has campaigned around the idea that young people should "build their ⁠futures here at home and prevent the continued exodus of young Cape Verdeans abroad”. She has also made the need for a balance of power central to her campaign.Neves belongs to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), which won a majority in May's parliamentary election, securing 37 of the 72 seats and ending a decade of MpD-led government. A Rosa victory would place the presidency and government in opposing political camps.Rosa is the first woman to contest the presidency since Cape Verde gained independence in 1975. While women have held senior cabinet positions, the country has never had a woman president or prime minister.Under Cape Verde's parliamentary-presidential system, the prime minister holds most executive authority, while the president has veto powers and a mediating role.Polling stations were scheduled to open at 8 am and close at 6 pm local time. Provisional results were expected within two or three days. If no candidate secures more than 50% of the vote, the two leading candidates will face each other in a runoff on November 29.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pat McFadden backs legal right to job support for young people
articles.summary: The work and pensions secretary said the level of support currently on offer was too vague.
articles.body:
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.

Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:

a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government

GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work

ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year .

articles.title: Redrawing Pakistan: Ministers back 12-province plan but political, constitutional hurdles remain
articles.summary: Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better
articles.body: Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better governance. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. Speaking to Geo News, he said the country could consider creating 12 provinces, provided the boundaries were drawn on administrative rather than linguistic, ethnic or political grounds.“If there is a proposal for 12 provinces, then make it 12,” Asif said, adding that new units should not be created to serve “language, ethnicity or political interests”.Pakistan’s interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also revived the debate, suggesting a referendum to gauge public opinion on the contentious issue. His remarks have fuelled speculation that powerful quarters favour a broader restructuring of Pakistan's administrative map, with reports pointing to a possible constitutional exercise in 2027.No formal roadmap, however, has been announced. The proposed number of provinces, their boundaries and the process for creating them remain undecided.What the proposed 12-province map could look likeOne proposal reported in Pakistani media envisages dividing Punjab into four provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan into three each, and Sindh into two. The plan could involve a nationwide referendum and a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, although neither has been confirmed as an approved government initiative.Supporters argue that the existing arrangement concentrates too much administrative and financial authority in provincial capitals leaving smaller cities and districts dependent on decisions taken far away.Asif has questioned whether federal funds transferred to provincial governments are reaching local institutions, arguing that decentralisation could bring decision-making and resources closer to communities. Advocates of the proposal say smaller provinces would make public services more accessible and help address uneven development.But the debate is not only about the size of administrative units. It also raises questions about whether creating more provinces would improve governance without stronger local governments and greater financial autonomy for districts.Political consensus remains the biggest hurdleThe proposal has exposed differences within the ruling coalition itself. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), led by Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, has firmly opposed any division of Sindh, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has yet to settle on a formal position.The two parties are coalition partners in the federal government. The PML-N has said it will announce its position if the matter comes before Parliament, despite some of its leaders backing the creation of smaller provinces.A cabinet member in the Shehbaz Sharif government said reaching agreement would be difficult without the support of the major political parties.The issue has also prompted speculation about a possible understanding between the government and the main opposition, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). PML-N leader and former federal minister Khawaja Saad Rafique has suggested that the establishment could offer relief to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in return for PTI's support for the proposed constitutional changes. There has been no confirmation of such a deal.Smaller parties have also entered the debate. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its demand for new administrative units in Sindh, while Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain has called for new provinces to be considered through consultation and in the national interest.The Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party has backed the proposal on administrative grounds, while Jamaat-i-Islami has argued that the creation of new provinces should go hand in hand with strengthening local governments.What the Constitution requiresEven if political parties agree on the broad idea, redrawing provincial boundaries would require a demanding constitutional process.Under Article 239 of Pakistan's Constitution, an amendment requires the support of at least two-thirds of the total membership of both houses of Parliament. If it changes the limits of an existing province, it must also secure the backing of at least two-thirds of the total membership of that province's assembly.That gives provincial parties considerable leverage over any proposed division.A nationwide referendum is not an automatic constitutional requirement for creating provinces. Any such exercise would need its own legal and constitutional basis, and Parliament could not simply be bypassed in deciding the process or framing the questions put to voters.Following a meeting between Pakistan’s president Asif Ali Zardari and prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday, a senior government official told news agency PTI that the two leaders had agreed to adhere strictly to the constitutional provisions governing the creation of new provinces. They also agreed that any proposed referendum would require parliamentary approval.Former federal information minister Muhammad Ali Durrani has meanwhile launched a campaign for the restoration of Bahawalpur province and the creation of 11 other smaller administrative units.For now, the proposal remains a subject of political debate rather than an agreed government plan. Any move to redraw the map would require agreement on boundaries, resources, parliamentary representation and the future of provincial institutions — as well as the constitutional numbers to make it happen.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas
articles.summary: Mansour Abbas faces mounting pressure from Israel’s change bloc to denounce Hamas as a prerequisite for coalition role.
articles.body:
The question of whether Mansour Abbas, the leader of Israel’s United Arab List (Ra’am), is willing to recognise the Palestinian group Hamas as a “terrorist” organisation may determine whether his party will play a role in the country’s next government.

According to Israel’s Ynet news website, Abbas has signalled to parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he would agree to the designation in exchange for a “genuine partnership” in a coalition led by Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming a new government after last month’s elections.

Eisenkot has made recognising Hamas as a “terrorist” group one of the conditions for joining his prospective coalition. He has also demanded that Abbas recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state – despite Abbas’s own identity as a Palestinian citizen of Israel.

But on Wednesday, Abbas denied that he had made a declaration on Hamas. Earlier in the week, he had simply reiterated Ra’am’s support for disarming Hamas, and condemning “terrorism”.

The demands concerning Hamas and recognising Israel as a Jewish state pose a problem for Abbas, whose party represents Palestinian citizens of Israel – around 20 percent of the population, excluding the millions who live under Israeli occupation in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

He wants to join the government – and has previously done so in the past, in 2021 – seeing it as a way to improve the lives of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and force Netanyahu and other far-right figures out of power.

But declaring Hamas a “terrorist” group would be seen by critics as tantamount to supporting the Israeli narrative, during a genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians.

Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera that Eisenkot’s conditions are intended to make a partnership with Ra’am more acceptable to his Jewish Israeli supporters and coalition partners.

“Eisenkot is telling them practically that Ra’am’s votes will help him form the government, and that this partnership will take place according to the definition he wants for the state,” Jabareen said.

Including Ra’am’s eight seats in parliament would go a long way to helping Eisenkot secure a viable coalition. His own bloc has 48 seats, but Ra’am and another Arab-led party, the Joint List, recommended him to lead the government . The Joint List, however, is more unlikely to agree to any of Eisenkot’s demands, and therefore if it does support the prospective prime minister, it will be from outside the government.

Political jockeying continues in Israel, with other factors – such as who the ultra-Orthodox parties will back, and how many of Eisenkot’s coalition partners will be willing to accept any role for Ra’am – complicating matters.

During consultations with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on November 5, Abbas was asked why he would not use the “terrorist” designation when describing Hamas. The Ra’am leader said he needed the “space to be a bridge” between Jews and Palestinians.

“Leave me also a space to protect myself and my family,” he added, saying it was an issue of “life and death”.

Jabareen warned of underlying tensions even if an agreement over the designation was reached.

“There is also a security dispute,” Jabareen said. “Signing the classification of Hamas does not determine how Ra’am will act if the government decides to resume a wide war in Gaza.”

Then there is the question of recognising Israel as a Jewish state. Abbas has previously accepted that as a political reality, saying in 2021 that the country had been established as a Jewish state. But this year he clarified that accepting that as a reality did not mean endorsing it.

“The Jewish character of the state is an existing fact that was imposed on us, and we did not choose it,” he wrote in August.

Jabareen said Abbas was trying to navigate a complex situation, ensuring that he reflects the positions and beliefs of his Palestinian base, while being more acceptable and palatable to the wider Israeli public. The analyst, however, feels that this may have gone too far in the latter direction.

“Abbas is trying to be the most loyal to the government… he is looking at the Israeli voter more than he looks at his own voter,” Jabareen said. “He took legitimacy from his voter, and now he must see how he can correct the course with the Israeli voter.”

The prospect of Ra’am joining an Eisenkot government has also been seized upon by Netanyahu, who has repeatedly focused on the perceived threat of parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, portraying them as a danger to the state.

However, reports have emerged that Netanyahu’s close associate and former chief of staff, Natan Eshel, has contacted Abbas to gauge his stance on supporting Eisenkot.

“Publicly, Netanyahu is trying to make Ra’am’s support more politically costly for Eisenkot to secure, whether by encouraging opposition among Eisenkot’s partners or by making Abbas less willing to support him without concessions,” Jabareen said.

Abbas’s options include joining Eisenkot’s coalition, supporting a minority government from outside, or joining the opposition.

“Supporting the government from outside it may reduce the cost of having an open partnership with Eisenkot, and give Abbas greater freedom to object to government decisions,” Jabareen said.

But there is another complication. Another leading member of Eisenkot’s bloc, Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, has repeatedly said he would oppose a minority government that is dependent on Arab-led parties.

Lieberman, a right-wing politician, has shown few signs of budging from his position, and has instead encouraged Eisenkot to partner with ultra-Orthodox parties – who were part of Netanyahu’s coalition during the last government – despite previous disputes over military conscription of Jewish religious students.

And then, even if Lieberman’s opposition is overcome, there is the potential for any future conflict, either with Palestinians or with regional states, to put any arrangement under strain, Jabareen warned.

“If it is just a short confrontation with Iran, then there is more of a chance of Abbas staying in any coalition,” Jabareen said. “But if it is a wider war in Gaza, or an escalation in Al-Aqsa or the West Bank, or even in Lebanon, that would put him under direct pressure from his supporters.”

Jabareen pointed to a similar dilemma in 2022, when Ra’am suspended its participation in the Israeli government coalition at the time over Israeli police raids and violence at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.

“Would Ra’am stay silent on those issues just to keep the coalition together?” Jabareen asked. “I expect it would first voice its objections and, if the escalation continued, suspend its participation.”

articles.title: Schoolboy imposter subjected former professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'
articles.summary: Brian MacKinnon - who posed as a school boy in his 30s - targeted a former university professor as he lay in bed with his wife.
articles.body:
An imposter who made headlines around the world for posing as a school pupil in his 30s has appeared in court and admitted hiding in the home of his former university professor before subjecting him to a "terrifying ordeal".

Brian MacKinnon targeted Prof Brian Whiting, 87, as he lay in bed with his wife, the day after a BBC docudrama on his ruse was broadcast.

My Old School chronicled MacKinnon's return to Bearsden Academy, as Brandon Lee, a 16-year-old who had supposedly just moved to Scotland from Canada.

MacKinnon hatched the plan so he could pursue his dream of becoming a doctor having been thrown out of Glasgow University, when Prof Whiting was dean of the medical school.

The model pupil who was a 30-year-old imposter

MacKinnon - who was formerly a pupil at the East Dunbartonshire school from 1974 to 1980 - returned in 1993 and secured five As in his Higher exams.

As a result he earned a place at the University of Dundee to study medicine.

But in 1995 an anonymous tip-off revealed he had previously spent two years as a medical student at the University of Glasgow and did not complete the course.

MacKinnon was thrown out of the medical school in 1983 following a failed appeal.

When his double life was exposed, Prof Whiting was interviewed by BBC Scotland News.

The archive footage was used in the 2022 docudrama, which starred Alan Cumming as MacKinnon.

Details of the case, which called before the High Court in Glasgow on Thursday, were first reported in the Mail on Sunday .

The court heard MacKinnon, now 63, went to the retired academic's home on 28 September last year - the day after My Old School had been repeated on the BBC.

It is believed MacKinnon sneaked into the property, in the west end of the city, around 16:30 as the rear door and gate were unlocked.

Prof Whiting was in his study and his 83-year-old wife, Marlene, was in the garden.

They went to bed around 23:30, unaware MacKinnon was hiding in their home.

About two hours later they were awoken when their room door suddenly opened.

A figure wearing dark clothes, a grey cap and a mask over the lower part of his face walked up to the side of the bed and told Marlene: "No lights."

Prosecutor Eilidh Robertson told the High Court in Glasgow: "She sat up and MacKinnon demanded that she lie back down or he would really hurt her.

"Both the Whitings were very frightened by this point.

"MacKinnon then pointed at her husband and asked: 'Is that Brian Whiting?'."

MacKinnon then said he had brought "two statements" which he wanted the couple to "release".

Robertson said MacKinnon threatened to kill the couple and hurt their families if they did not comply.

Marlene did not know who the intruder was before he said his name was "Brian MacKinnon".

Robertson added: "MacKinnon then spoke to Brian Whiting directly blaming him and two colleagues for ruining his life and having responsibility for the death of his parents."

MacKinnon then briefly left the room and, on his return, suddenly asked to be let out the house.

Marlene got up and led him downstairs hoping he would go.

She asked how he had initially got in, he boasted: "That was easy."

Marlene got a good look at MacKinnon after he took off his mask.

The advocate depute said: "She unlocked the front door.

"As MacKinnon was leaving, he stated that he had people working for him that would check if the witnesses were complying with his demands.

"If not, they would be dead. He then left the house and turned down a lane."

He went on to show her an online photo of MacKinnon and she identified him as the man who had invaded their home.

The court heard how the two statements left by MacKinnon had been made to look as if they had been completed by Prof Whiting.

Each alleged the retired dean had "succumbed to intolerable pressure to make a misleading statement about Brian Lachlan MacKinnon".

They also said: "Via a BBC Scotland television broadcast, I stated falsely that MacKinnon had not met the required standard as a medical student after he had set out to study medicine at Glasgow in 1980. Nothing could have been further from the truth."

The documents claimed there had been a "conspiracy" to exclude "incandescently bright" students like MacKinnon.

They also included "defamatory" remarks about Glasgow University, BBC Scotland and Alan Cumming.

MacKinnon was not initially traced but DNA recovered at the house helped link him to the crime.

CCTV from a nearby property had also captured him walking near the Whitings property that afternoon.

MacKinnon was eventually arrested as he returned to his home in Milngavie, East Dunbartonshire, hours after the incident.

Police Scotland officers went on to recover a mobile phone and three notepads.

In one, there was handwritten text which stated: "I will regain a place to study medicine at a reputable university".

An envelope was also seized and a "statement" similar to those given to the Whitings was discovered inside.

MacKinnon made no comment when quizzed by detectives.

Last week he was brought into court in a wheelchair and pleaded guilty to a charge of attempted extortion.

Sean Templeton, defending, told the hearing: "It is clear that he has had an extraordinary life, thrust into the public gaze in the 1990s by attending a school when he was over the age of 18."

He added MacKinnon had always wanted to be involved in medicine to "assist the public", but his "ambitions to become a doctor came to an end".

Templeton said after he was exposed, it had "characterised" his life in the many years since, including the docudrama which MacKinnon "did not agree to".

The defence advocate said: "It is something that has dogged him since the 1990s."

MacKinnon had been assessed by a psychiatrist after his initial appearance in court in late September last year, but it was eventually concluded that he was "fit to stand trial".

Templeton told the court MacKinnon was "frail" and suffered from uncontrolled movements in one of his arms.

Lady Anwar continued his remand in custody as sentencing was deferred for reports until a later date.

MacKinnon is currently being held at HMP Barlinnie in Glasgow.

She told him: "You subjected Mr and Mrs Whiting, both in their 80s, to a shocking and terrifying ordeal in their home.

"It is likely you will face a significant custodial sentence."

articles.title: Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly church attack
articles.summary: Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death on Sunday for carrying out an attack ​on a church in the southern governorate of ‌Karak last month that killed nine people, the state news agency Petra reported.
articles.body: AMMAN — Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death on Sunday for carrying out an attack ​on a church in the southern governorate of ‌Karak last month that killed nine people, the state news agency Petra reported. The court convicted the men of offences including ​carrying out terrorist acts resulting in death, possessing ​weapons and ammunition for terrorist purposes and promoting ⁠the ideology of a terrorist group. The ruling ​is subject to appeal and automatic review by the ​Court of Cassation, Petra said. Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud on ​October 23, in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian ​minority. Authorities said 34 people were also wounded. Security forces arrested the ‌three ⁠men on October 26 after a shootout at an abandoned house in Karak. All three were wounded, while no security personnel were injured, according to the ​Public Security Directorate. Jordan, ​a U.S. ⁠partner in the fight against extremism, later that day launched airstrikes on southern Syria against groups ​it linked to the church attack. Syrian ​authorities ⁠said seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed. Jordan later acknowledged that its airstrikes had killed ⁠civilians ​in Syria and the two countries agreed ​to form a joint security committee to review the incident and its ​consequences.

articles.title: Eleven officers convicted of crimes still on police payroll, chief confirms
articles.summary: Police Scotland Chief Constable Jo Farrell said there were other cases with "incontrovertible evidence" against officers, but they cannot be sacked quickly enough.
articles.body:
Eleven officers who have been convicted of crimes - including eight who have been violent towards women and girls - are still on the Police Scotland pay roll.

In a letter to the Scottish Parliament's justice committee, Chief Constable Jo Farrell said there were other cases with "incontrovertible evidence" against officers, but they cannot be sacked quickly enough.

Farrell also said the £4.5m annual cost of the 80 officers who are currently suspended was down to "sluggish" conduct arrangements, as well as the time necessary for cases to go through courts.

She described the state of affairs as "intolerable" and called for a modernisation of the police conduct regime.

The revelation follows a number of high-profile cases of police officers who have been exposed as rapists this year alone.

Derek McNee , Campbell Petrie , Carmichael John Williamson and Cameron Ross have all been convicted and are no longer on the payroll.

Meanwhile, Alan Greer , who was named as a violent serial rapist by a BBC investigation, took his own life in May after police raided his home.

It also emerged last month that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

Farrell wrote the letter to justice committee convener David Linden ahead of a meeting this week.

She said: "There are cases of proven criminality where the existing process has taken too long because of sub-optimal regulations.

"This can leave individuals who ultimately have no place in policing within the organisation for longer than they should be."

She continued: "There are other cases where there is incontrovertible evidence against officers which cannot be fast-tracked for dismissal under current arrangements.

"This is intolerable to me, as Chief Constable, and would rightly be intolerable to the public."

That officers remain suspended for years, she said, has a "welfare impact, a cost to the public purse, and reduce policing's overall deployable resource".

Last month, Farrell said that between 300 and 400 officers had now been re-vetted as part of new rules brought in following the murder of Sarah Everard by Met Police officer Wayne Couzens .

Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women

Misconduct probe after police officer admits abusing woman

The committee will be discussing options that will allow Police Scotland to act quicker in cases where there are convictions.

Farrell said the proposals under consideration would "modernise the police conduct regime, to accelerate hearings for the most serious cases and enhance transparency of outcomes".

"I strongly support the focus on treating witnesses and complainers in a trauma-informed way," she said.

Justice Secretary Neil Gray said: "The Chief Constable is right that cases involving officers convicted of serious offences should be dealt with more quickly.

"This is why we have introduced regulations to Parliament that will allow Police Scotland to act quicker in cases where there are convictions."

He added: "These are aimed at improving transparency and strengthening support for victims and witnesses, while retaining appropriate safeguards."

articles.title: CHUCK DEVORE: Texas turns blue, but here’s where the next 4 big battles are coming
articles.summary: Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa's new agenda could reshape Texas on taxes, spending, regulation, DEI policy, border security and Operation Lone Star.
articles.body: After November’s election verdict, Texas isn’t doomed to become California overnight — but not for a lack of trying. As in much of America (Florida excepted), Texas saw major midterm losses for a Republican Party that has dominated the Lone Star State for the past quarter century. Inauguration Day in 2027, all statewide executive offices were held by Republicans — now the opposite will be the case. Democrats took the state House of Representatives, but Republicans still hold the state Senate. Republicans also retain a one-vote margin on the state Supreme Court, and the state’s powerful Railroad Commission (the agency that regulates the oil and gas industry, gas utilities, pipeline safety and surface coal and uranium mining) will have a 2-to-1 Republican majority. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa will bring Texans an entirely new set of priorities and a vastly different style of governance. She began her career as a labor attorney, including working for a powerful government union. In 2005, she was on the legal team that pursued lawfare against then-Republican House Majority Leader Tom DeLay on money-laundering charges. DeLay was driven from office, convicted in 2010 and fully acquitted in 2014 — the process is the punishment. Before her election to the Texas House in 2016, Hinojosa served on the board of trustees for the Austin Independent School District, a district that has struggled with declining enrollment and the threat of state takeover after campuses received five consecutive failing accountability ratings. How might Texas under Hinojosa’s leadership fare? Here are four things to watch. 1. Taxes and spending TEXAS GOVERNOR-ELECT'S PLAN TO FREEZE ELECTRICITY PRICES RAISES QUESTIONS OVER LEGAL AUTHORITY For decades, Texas has benefited from lower taxes and a smaller, less intrusive government than peer-state rivals such as California, Illinois and New York. The population has soared as millions of Americans — and foreign nationals — sought opportunity. That is unlikely to change overnight. What is likely is incremental slippage as other states, notably Florida and Tennessee, work to attract talent and investment. 2. Regulation and lawsuit climate 11TH-HOUR POWER PLAY TARGETS INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR AFTER HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT Texas last passed major tort reform in 2003 and has seen its national lawsuit-climate ranking slip since then. Hinojosa’s ascent likely means a gradual strengthening of the state’s trial bar at the expense of economic growth. Ironically, it will likely also increase the cost of living — with affordability an explicit promise of the incoming Democratic leadership. Further, Texas’s innovative Business Court and the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, both created in 2023, saw all three Republican members of the Fifteenth Court lose to Democrats. This flip may tilt the landscape against larger employers when interpreting the scope and power of state regulatory actions. ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE Hinojosa has already moved against billionaire Elon Musk’s plans to expand SpaceX’s Starbase site in Cameron County. Given the governor-elect was part of the lawfare posse that destroyed DeLay, will Hinojosa and her lieutenants resist the urge to go after Musk personally at the risk of harming job creation and innovation in Texas? 3. Culture and higher education Here is where Hinojosa’s victory may have a significant long-term effect. She is positioned to reverse strictures that banned the use of so-called diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) in hiring and curriculum, especially in the university system. Her appointments to higher-education governing boards could reverse many of the commonsense gains made under outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, including the 2023 ban on DEI offices and related practices. 4. Border security HOUSTON MAYOR BOLTS EARLY FROM ICE COOPERATION AFTER BLUE WAVE CRASHES IN TEXAS Here Hinojosa’s campaign promises could have an immediate and dramatic effect. Texas has worked alongside the federal government under Republican President Donald Trump, and in spite of the federal government under former Democrat President Joe Biden, to secure its roughly 1,254-mile border with Mexico. Texas last passed major tort reform in 2003 and has seen its national lawsuit-climate ranking slip since then. Hinojosa’s ascent likely means a gradual strengthening of the state’s trial bar at the expense of economic growth. The state’s effort — with National Guard soldiers and Department of Public Safety troopers — aims to protect Texans’ health and welfare by interdicting transnational human smuggling and drug-cartel operations, which include the use of increasingly sophisticated and deadly drones. BORDER DEM POISED TO WIELD ICE PURSE STRINGS REJECTS SOCIALIST ‘DEFUND’ PUSH The federal government has some 12,000 to 19,000 Border Patrol, Customs, DEA and active-duty military personnel deployed along the border in Texas at any given time. The state of Texas, through Operation Lone Star, has augmented that with up to 5,500 Guard soldiers and 1,600 DPS troopers for a total of up to 7,000 personnel — meaning Texas provides about one out of every two people guarding the long Rio Grande frontier. articles.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as company conducts internal probe over Nvidia fallout
articles.summary: Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO...
articles.body:
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence." It did not address specific allegations.

"The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," it said in an emailed statement.

Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company," the statement said. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters."

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia , Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was "no evidence" of illicit chip transfers.

Singapore's government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible "false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers."

Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed's then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided "inaccurate" information to downplay her role at the company.

An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.

As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: "I don't know if that's been determined yet."

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.

The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.

The company's finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.

In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan's name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws "extremely seriously."

The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

articles.title: Gaza families bury bodies of loved ones trapped for years under rubble
articles.summary: The remains of 69 Palestinians have been recovered in northern Gaza, allowing families to bury them.
articles.body:
Jabalia, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Nabhan, a man in his sixties from Bir an-Naaja in northern Gaza, had waited more than three years for this day.

He wanted to give his loved ones a proper burial after 17 members of his family, including his seven children and grandchildren, were killed when their home was targeted 20 days after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Among those killed was Nabhan’s 45-day-old grandchild.

After years of searching for their bodies, on Sunday Nabhan was finally able to bury his family members after Civil Defence teams retrieved their remains from the rubble of his home.

“All of them were children, all of them were loved ones,” he said.

Nabhan said there had been no fighters, Israeli soldiers or captives inside the home when it was struck.

For the past three years, he had tried to help recover his family’s remains, but the difficult conditions prevented this.

Their recovery from his destroyed home brought some relief for Nabhan, but it also brought more trauma.

“It feels as if they have just been killed again. The wounds have reopened,” he said. “But, thank God, we now know that our children have a grave here, beside their siblings, and we can visit them.”

The genocide in Gaza killed at least 73,600 people, with 82 per cent of the structures in Gaza damaged and two-thirds of them destroyed by waves of Israeli air strikes and shelling.

Under the rubble were thousands of bodies, with the continued attacks by Israeli forces often making it too dangerous for families or Civil Defence teams to retrieve them.

A truce agreed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, which has been repeatedly broken by Israel, has allowed for some of the bodies to be recovered from the rubble that carpets Gaza

Civil Defence teams have managed to retrieve the remains of 69 Palestinians from locations in Jabalia refugee camp and Beit Lahiya in recent days.

For many families, the operation marked the end of years of uncertainty. Relatives had repeatedly followed up with Civil Defence, waiting for heavy machinery and other equipment to reach bodies trapped under collapsed buildings.

Fatima al-Masri, 47, said her husband and 18-year-old son were killed in an Israeli attack in the Safatwi area of northern Gaza in October 2024. Their remains have been buried beneath the rubble of their home for two years.

“Every month, every two months, sometimes every week or every two weeks, we would follow up with Civil Defence,” she said. “They told us they needed heavy equipment to lift the house because several floors had collapsed on top of them.”

After a long delay, the recovery operation began, with workers digging through the rubble using machines and by hand. They found bone fragments and al-Masri’s son’s mobile phone, along with the bodies and belongings of those who had been with her husband and son.

“Thank God, we found their remains and everything that was with them,” al-Masri said.

The two years of tortuous delays had left her in a constant state of anxiety. Every day, the same questions occupied her thoughts.

“I was always tense and worried. Every day, the same question was in my mind: ‘When would they recover them? When would we be able to bring them out?’” she said.

After the remains were recovered, she expressed relief that her husband and son could finally be buried.

The Palestinian Civil Defence estimates that more than 8,000 bodies are still to be recovered across Gaza.

The total number of missing Palestinians is estimated to exceed 10,000, although the broader figure includes people whose whereabouts remain unknown for different reasons, including those believed to be buried under rubble, detained or buried without identification.

Israel’s ongoing siege on Gaza means that Civil Defence teams have limited resources, with manual excavation often the only way to do their grim work.

According to Palestinian authorities cited by the United Nations, more than 630 bodies and human remains had been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025 by September 2026.

Ramiz Hassouna, a lecturer at Israa University, said the recovery of his brother’s remains, Montaser, brought nearly two years of uncertainty to an end.

He disappeared on November 8, 2024, during the Israeli military siege of Jabalia refugee camp. He was last known to be in the al-Faluja area, where he had been trapped with a group of friends.

For almost two years, the family received conflicting accounts about his fate. Some said he had been killed, while others believed he had been detained.

The uncertainty ended when Civil Defence teams recovered his remains from a destroyed building in al-Faluja and contacted the family. He was identified through personal belongings, including his wristwatch, a miswak (a traditional teeth-cleaning stick) and a prayer booklet, as well as distinctive marks on his front teeth.

Hassouna could not bring himself to go and identify his brother’s remains, so asked his younger brother to go in his place.

“I personally could not bear to look at my brother in that condition. I left it to my younger brother to identify him,” he said.

The remains of the friends Montaser was with when he died were recovered together and buried in the same grave.

“As they accompanied one another in this life, they will accompany one another in the afterlife,” said Hassouna.

On Sunday, he said the upgrades already under way should be completed in one push rather than through what he called “drips and drabs”.“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote on his social media platform, describing the existing system as around 50 years old. articles.title: Record number of migrants arrive in Spain’s Canary Islands
articles.summary: New EU migration and asylum laws have largely failed to stem flow of migrants to Spain and its territories.
articles.body:
Spain has declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.

Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, also known as pirogues, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on Saturday.

That’s broken the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is visiting ⁠El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.

Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from El Hierro, said the arrival this year has set a record in the 32 years since statistics have been collected.

“There’s been even more arrivals by Sunday afternoon”, Smith said, adding that the new arrivals are processed at the port in El Hierro and taken to a reception centre and sent on to other Canary Islands or to the Spanish mainland.

The European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum officially came into force on June 12, 2026, introducing “firm and fair rules” for accepting asylum requests, marking the most sweeping overhaul of EU asylum and border laws in decades.

“EU states are under pressure to do more to control migration from Africa and from outside the European Union,” Smith said, adding that the new rules haven’t stopped the flow of migrants to Spain and its enclaves.

Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who had entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July.

At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.

Most of the migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, many leaving from Senegal, with hopes of reaching mainland Europe.

But to get there, they risk their lives in small, often overcrowded boats at sea.

One boat on Saturday was carrying 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children, authorities said.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first 10 months of 2026.

“It is a treacherous journey,” said Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque, reporting from Dakar in Senegal, from where some of the boats depart, adding that favourable weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean have made departures from the coastlines in Africa much easier in recent years.

“So when the weather conditions allow it, the boats go out there,” he said, noting that migrants use “wooden fishing vessels called pirogues” in which up to 100 people are packed in for “a journey that can last one week”.

articles.title: Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
articles.summary: Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could squeeze militias and avert internal strife
articles.body:
The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.

The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.

At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.

For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.

That led Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to launch the crackdown, with an Iraqi security committee entering Jurf al-Nasr on Friday to investigate, following the arrest of other officials accused of graft. The formerly Sunni-majority area has long been considered outside government control since Iraqi militias seized the area a decade ago.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at Horizon Engage, told Al Jazeera that Jurf al-Sakhar’s value is deeply rooted in recent developments in Iraq, when Iran-linked militias used the campaign against ISIL (ISIS) to stamp their authority in the country.

“Iran-backed militias illegally seized and renamed Jurf al-Sakr when they conducted sectarian cleansing of the Sunni residents in the area in 2014, under the cover of the anti-Daesh [ISIL] war,” Knights explained.

The town, about 60km (37 miles) from Baghdad, is at a critical point near the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and Karbala.

It was once the site of Saddam Hussein’s military industrial complexes, which made Jurf al-Nasr an ideal place for Iraqi militias to test, build and hide rockets, drones and missiles, said Knights.

“If full control is taken, which is unlikely, the government would be able to finally tell Iraqis that a militia had been removed from its base and the legal residents of the area allowed to return,” he said. “This would be like taking back the Bekaa Valley from Hezbollah.”

Knights said the actual financial impact on Kataib Hezbollah of the Jurf al-Sakhar crackdown could be less spectacular than expected, with the militia having other sources of revenue.

Analysts say that dismantling the smuggling networks is part of a wider project to bring weapons under the control of the state.

After some Iran-linked militias missed a deadline to disarm this year, PM al-Zaidi now appears to be using economic pressure to weaken these armed groups without directly confronting them.

Security and strategic expert Saif Raad told Al Jazeera that the anticorruption campaign in Jurf al-Sakhar is essentially a message from the PM that no group is above the law.

“This duality is over. Part of what happened now is that the Iraqi people knew these factions and knew why they hold onto weapons, and I believe this is a victory achieved by the government without a single drop of Iraqi blood,” Raad said.

“Jurf al-Sakhar has been around for, let’s say, more than ten years; for ten years no prime minister was able to enter this area.”

A central focus of the government’s strategy is executing this crackdown without igniting a potentially explosive ‘Shia-on-Shia’ armed conflict.

The militia network which emerged following the US-led invasion of Iraq – and was emboldened during the campaign against ISIL – includes groups with widely divergent political and religious views. Some are closely aligned to Iran and accused of being proxies of Tehran, while others are closer to the federal government.

In a bid to prevent violence, Al-Zaidi reportedly cooperated with leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), particularly with the Badr Organisation, before initiating the arrests and dismissals in Jurf al-Sakhar, Raad said.

Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that leveraging Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organisation, was essential to neutralising the threat from the militias.

“The Badr Organisation is considered the largest combat force within the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so the process of focusing on this issue… is a fundamental part of strengthening the state project,” Raad observed.

“[The campaign] is a major shift in the process of strengthening the state and state institutions and making the Popular Mobilisation Forces an active and large part in controlling these groups [militias outside government control].”

Political analyst Ali Fadhlallah said that due to the structural nature of Iraq’s political and religious leadership, an internal war between the Shia factions was never likely to break out, particularly due to the influence Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani.

“The Shia component has very many large and positive factors that serve as a brake for any clash that is supposed to happen,” Fadhlallah said.

“The presence of the rational religious authority, which has always controlled the rhythm of the political process at dangerous crossroads, definitely has a very large role and it is monitoring the events… the issue of a [Shia-Shia] clash is unlikely, even in the most difficult and miserable circumstances.”

articles.title: Billie Piper to star in horror set in 'old iron Welsh town'
articles.summary: Welsh filmmaker Jamie Jones hopes it will tap into "important and real issues".
articles.body:
Actor Billie Piper is set to star in a new supernatural horror filmed on the "outskirts of an old iron town" in Wales.

Located "somewhere on the perimeter" of Merthyr Tydfil or Aberdare, Sketchbook will feature Piper, alongside child actor Woody Norman, as a mother and son who are reunited after years apart in foster care.

It will be directed by Swansea-born filmmaker Jamie Jones, who hopes the film will tap into "important and real issues" while still providing the thrill of a horror.

"I think a lot of people will relate to the issues, of growing up and social exclusion, going on beneath it all - but on the surface it's a really exciting horror film," he said.

Jones, who received a BAFTA Cymru breakthrough award for his work on his feature debut Obey, said he wanted the film to be dark, fun, tense and exciting, but also have substance.

"There needs to be something meaty you can chew on and there is that with this, in abundance."

The film starts in foster care and follows the son returning home to his mum, Piper - a single, working class mother "struggling to cope".

"Because his mother wasn't coping, she needed a bit of support and a bit or a break from him," said Jones.

"The sense of rejection he feels is then when the horror genre then starts to seep into the narrative.

"This horror then starts to unfold is kind of like a metaphor for families that are in impossible situations."

Jones said he drew upon "real social experiences to drive the narrative", including his own experiences with mental health, neurodiversity and systematic care.

A sketchbook acts as a form of physical expression and a "safe place" for the son as he sketches out his emotions.

"He draws ultimately as a way of expressing himself and to feel like he has some form of control," said Jones.

"The way that the narrative unfolds, the two things crash together, so to speak. Which I think is a really fun journey for viewers to go on... it's a roller coaster ride."

It will be the latest film for Piper, who is known for roles in BBC's Doctor Who, Secret Diary of a Call Girl and the Netflix series Collateral.

Jones said Piper's performance in the psychological drama Two for Joy inspired his decision for her to star as the mother.

"I've always loved Billie Piper and I think she's had a fabulous life and career," he added.

"She is the salt of the Earth, you know, she's very warm, she's very loyal, she's got all of these great qualities, but she's struggling.

"When the odds are stacked against you, it's tough, you know. You've just got to try your best, and that's what her character does.

"It just felt like the perfect role for Billie."

Lots of details are yet to be ironed out, but filming is set to start in February.

Despite being set in Wales, Jones is undecided if Piper and Norman will have to adopt a Welsh accent, as the characters nationality does not play a huge role in the film.

"It's not necessarily about being Welsh, or about Wales, per say, but I want to set it in Wales because that's where I'm from.

"I would like to do that as much as possible, if you're from somewhere, I think it's good to set things in a place you know and you know the texture, the nuances and the humour.

"Which helps make it all entertaining. I wanted to get the visual language of the old iron towns in there... but I'm not going to locate it specifically."

He said he sees a lot of the themes, including class divides, to be universally understood and the setting will help him give the film a grit he understands.

"The setting is important, and where they are, and the world and community is important," said Jones.

"But what's important is that they are working class or struggling. The more you talk about universal themes, the bigger your audience can be, and you can bring your audience in to a story that is also set in Wales.

"The Welsh thing can sneak under the hood. "I think that's only a good thing for Wales."

articles.title: In 2016, Nevada rancher David Park began protecting Desert Creek Ranch; its 1,228 acres are now permanently conserved for agriculture and sage-grouse habitat, and a 2026 grant will treat invasive grass on 350 acres
articles.summary: A Nevada rancher has permanently protected 1,228 acres of land to support farming and safeguard habitat for the rare Bi-State sage-grouse.
articles.body: A Nevada rancher has permanently protected 1,228 acres of land to support farming and safeguard habitat for the rare Bi-State sage-grouse. David Park began efforts to conserve Desert Creek Ranch in 2016, according to the Eastern Sierra Land Trust. The work has now resulted in a permanent conservation agreement covering the entire 1,228 acres. The agreement prevents non-agricultural development and protects the land as both working ranchland and wildlife habitat. A separate grant awarded in 2026 will also support restoration work across 350 acres of the property. The funding will be used to treat invasive grass, which threatens native plants and increases the risk of wildfires.A decade of protective effortRancher David Park began working to protect Desert Creek Ranch around ten years ago. His aim was to keep the property available for agriculture while protecting the natural areas needed by the Bi-State sage-grouse. According to documents from the Eastern Sierra Land Trust, the protection was achieved through a conservation easement. This is a legally binding agreement attached to a property's deed. It places permanent limits on how the land can be used, even when ownership changes. Under the agreement, the 1,228 acres cannot be used for non-agricultural development or divided into smaller plots. This prevents the land from being turned into residential or commercial developments. Park will continue to own the ranch and carry out livestock grazing. However, future owners will also have to follow the same restrictions because the agreement remains in place permanently. The Eastern Sierra Land Trust said Park wanted to make sure the ranch remained a working agricultural property while protecting important habitat for the rare sage-grouse population. The agreement is the result of years of planning and cooperation. It gives the land lasting protection while allowing Park to continue his ranching activities.Vital habitat for sage-grouseDesert Creek Ranch has been identified as important habitat for the Bi-State sage-grouse. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, these birds are a separate population of the greater sage-grouse. They are found only along the border between Nevada and California. The Bi-State sage-grouse is considered a sensitive species. Conservation efforts aim to protect its population and habitat to reduce the risk of it needing protection under the Endangered Species Act. The birds depend on large areas of connected land with native sagebrush, perennial grasses and wildflowers. These plants provide food, shelter and suitable places for nesting. They also need different types of habitat throughout the year. In spring, male sage-grouse gather in open areas called "leks" to perform mating displays. Females need thick sagebrush cover to build nests, while the plants also provide shelter during winter. During summer, females take their chicks to wet meadows and wetlands, where they can find insects and nutritious plants. According to the Eastern Sierra Land Trust, Desert Creek Ranch contains rare wet meadows and spring-fed areas that are important to the birds. These wet areas are particularly important because water and suitable wetland habitat are limited in the dry region. They provide food and shelter for young birds during a key stage of their development. Protecting these areas is therefore an important part of regional plans to conserve the Bi-State sage-grouse and support its long-term survival.Fighting invasive grass and fireA separate grant awarded in 2026 will pay for restoration work across 350 acres of the protected ranch. The Eastern Sierra Land Trust confirmed that the funding will be used to control invasive grass. Although the grant information does not identify the exact species, cheatgrass is one of the main invasive plants threatening Nevada's sagebrush areas, according to documents from the Nevada Department of Wildlife. Cheatgrass, scientifically known as Bromus tectorum, is a non-native annual grass that spreads quickly and competes with native plants. The U.S. Geological Survey has explained that the grass can also change the natural fire cycle across western landscapes. Native perennial grasses usually grow in separate clusters, leaving spaces of bare ground between them. Cheatgrass can fill these gaps, creating large areas of closely packed dry vegetation that provide fuel for fires. The grass dries out early in summer. This makes it easier for lightning strikes or human activity to start wildfires that can spread quickly.After a fire, cheatgrass can grow back rapidly. Native sagebrush, however, is often destroyed and can take decades to return. This creates a serious problem for sage-grouse because the birds depend on sagebrush for food, nesting and shelter. Cheatgrass also competes with native grasses and wildflowers, reducing the variety of plants available to wildlife and livestock. The 350-acre restoration project is intended to reduce these threats. Common control methods include applying herbicides before the grass grows, using carefully managed livestock grazing and planting native species again. The treatment will help restore the natural balance of vegetation and reduce the amount of dry grass that can fuel wildfires. By addressing invasive grass across 350 acres, the project will also help protect the wider 1,228-acre ranch. This adds another layer of protection for Park's livestock and the habitat used by the Bi-State sage-grouse.Keeping the ranch workingA major part of the conservation agreement is making sure Desert Creek Ranch can continue operating as a working agricultural property. The protection does not require Park to stop raising livestock. Instead, it aims to support ranching while maintaining the natural conditions needed by wildlife. Regional agricultural advocates have said that livestock production and sage-grouse conservation can work together. Carefully managed grazing can help control vegetation and maintain grassland health. According to state documents, appropriate grazing practices can also support wet meadows and keep grassland plants useful as food for both cattle and wildlife.The conservation easement prevents the property from being divided into residential or commercial plots. It also restricts uses that are not related to agriculture or open space. These limits are designed to protect the land's soil, water and natural resources. They also help ensure that the high desert property is not lost to large-scale development. Park will continue managing the ranch under stewardship plans that aim to balance agricultural production with wildlife habitat protection, according to the Eastern Sierra Land Trust. The permanent agreement means these protections will remain in place even if the ranch changes hands in the future. The 2026 restoration grant will further support that effort by addressing invasive grass across part of the property. Together, the conservation easement and restoration work aim to keep Desert Creek Ranch productive for agriculture while protecting an important part of the Bi-State sage-grouse's remaining habitat.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cruise passengers sharply divided over cutting buffet lines to sneak quick bites
articles.summary: Etiquette expert Diane Gottsman of Texas reveals why grabbing just one item while on a cruise ship buffet line still counts as cutting — and when rare exceptions apply.
articles.body: A common cruise ship buffet habit is raising questions — and eyebrows — about what passengers should and shouldn't do while filling their plates during meals. Cutting ahead of others to grab just one item may seem a harmless action, but it can frustrate fellow passengers who have been patiently waiting their turn. Buffet line-cutting was recently highlighted in a discussion about etiquette while at sea, according to the "Royal Caribbean Blog." CRUISE BUFFET GUESTS FACE SURPRISE CHARGES FOR TAKING FOOD BACK TO CABINS Passengers should wait their turn even if they only want something quick, such as a piece of toast or fruit, rather than squeezing past others or reaching around them, the blog advised. Jumping ahead generally sends the wrong message, said Diane Gottsman, an etiquette expert based in Texas. "It's never acceptable to jump in front of someone in a buffet line, whether on a cruise ship, at a restaurant buffet or at a wedding," Gottsman said. "Everyone is waiting their turn, so having someone jump in front of you comes across as rude," she added. "It also disrupts the flow of the buffet line, and in some cases can even cause a buffet traffic jam." CRUISE PASSENGERS CRITICIZE NEW PROGRAM IDENTIFYING EARLY TIPPERS ON BOARD There may be exceptions, however, depending on what someone needs and how crowded the buffet may be. Gottsman said reaching in for a napkin is more understandable than cutting ahead to grab food. If only a few people are waiting, politely asking to step in briefly for a fork or knife may also be acceptable. Another breach of etiquette Holding a place for someone else can also test the patience of passengers who have been waiting. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "If you're holding a space for your spouse, a friend or a child, the child generally gets a pass," said Gottsman. But the spouse and friend are probably being judged and frustrating others who have been standing in line for 20 or 30 minutes." If another passenger does cut the line, however, Gottsman generally advises against confronting the person over a minor offense. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES For someone who repeatedly jumps ahead, she suggested speaking with a manager in the dining area and allowing staff to handle the situation. Cruise passengers themselves appear divided over exactly where to draw the line. In a Reddit discussion, a traveler asked whether it was acceptable to skip ahead when people were waiting for the first dish at a buffet, but there was no line for other items farther down. "If there's a wide opening, it's fine. If you're squeezing in between people, then go wait in line like everyone else," one person wrote. articles.title: Jersey book swap scheme aims to inspire more young readers
articles.summary: Every Child Our Future has launched a book box exchange in Jersey as part of its literacy campaign.
articles.body:
A Jersey charity has created a book exchange box as part of a bid to encourage children to take up reading.

Every Child Our Future said the scheme would operate in a take-a-book, leave-a-book style system.

It said by sharing books in this way, stories that had been loved by one child could find a new home with another, giving more children the chance to discover the pleasure of reading.

The charity's chief executive Cris Lakeman said she wanted to "make reading accessible and something that children feel excited about".

The initiative forms part of the charity's 10th anniversary celebrations and its Big Jersey Read campaign, which aims to raise awareness of the importance of children's literacy.

The book exchange box was unveiled at De Gruchy's Arcade in St Helier, and it will be moved temporarily to the St Helier Methodist Centre, with the charity planning to take it to other venues across the island.

Lakeman said she hoped the box would "encourage families to share books, discover new stories and, most importantly, inspire more children to become lifelong readers".

articles.title: Thousands rally against Czech government's plan to switch public media funding
articles.summary: Protesters say the move will stifle media freedom, while the coalition government insists broadcasters need to cut costs.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the license fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44, £7.06) a month for Czech TV and Czech radio.

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence in 1993.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Večerníček, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.

Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.

"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.
