articles.title: 'Well-planned conspiracy': BJP refutes reports of 209-candidate list for upcoming UP elections
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Uttar Pradesh unit of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Sunday rejected reports claiming that a list of 209 candidates for the 2027
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Uttar Pradesh unit of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Sunday rejected reports claiming that a list of 209 candidates for the 2027 assembly elections had been prepared and sent to the party's central leadership, calling them fabricated and part of a "well-planned conspiracy"."For the past few days, certain media outlets, individuals, and institutions have been continuously circulating news regarding an alleged list of 209 candidates of the Bharatiya Janata Party, Uttar Pradesh, being prepared and sent to the central leadership in the context of the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. This is completely untrue, baseless, imaginary, and fabricated. The BJP outrightly refutes this fake and false news," news agency ANI quoted the statement as saying.Describing the reports as a "well-planned conspiracy", the statement alleged that some people were spreading rumours to create confusion, uncertainty and fear among party workers. It urged office-bearers, workers and the public not to rely on unverified reports and to follow information shared through authorised party platforms.The party said its candidate selection process had not yet begun. It added that the BJP follows a structured organisational process for choosing candidates for assembly and other elections.The joint statement was signed by chief minister Yogi Adityanath and state BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary.Earlier on Sunday, Chaudhary had also denied that the BJP had finalised names for 209 constituencies. Speaking to reporters, he said he had not held any meetings to prepare such a list.“I do not know the source of this news... As the State President of the Bharatiya Janata Party, I have not held any such meetings with anyone,” Chaudhary said.He outlined the party's candidate selection procedure, saying inputs are first collected at the district and regional levels before being discussed by the state core committee and election committee. The recommendations are then sent to Delhi, where the Parliamentary Board takes the final call.“The BJP is not a family-run party where a single individual can make such decisions; rather, the process is entirely collective,” he said.Chaudhary added that the party had followed the same organisational approach for the past 50 years, with decisions taken through consultation and consensus.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2016, Caden Smiley returned to his family’s South Dakota ranch; a decade later, he and wife Jori report greater plant and wildlife diversity after adopting rotational grazing and satellite-linked fencing
articles.summary: A ranching family in South Dakota has reported a major increase in plant and wildlife diversity after changing how they manage their cattle.
articles.body: A ranching family in South Dakota has reported a major increase in plant and wildlife diversity after changing how they manage their cattle. Nearly a decade after adopting rotational grazing and satellite-based fencing, Caden and Jori Smiley say their land has healthier grass, more plant varieties and a growing number of wild animals. Caden Smiley returned to his family's ranch near Kadoka, South Dakota, in 2016. He and his wife, Jori, later moved away from traditional grazing methods and introduced a system that allows grasslands to recover between periods of grazing. In a report to the Tri-State Neighbor, the couple said the changes, supported by virtual fencing technology, have improved the condition of their pastures and helped wildlife return to the ranch.A technological shift in pasturesThe biggest change at Smiley Ranch has been the move to rotational grazing. Instead of allowing cattle to feed in the same pasture throughout the season, the system moves them between different sections of land. When Caden returned to the family ranch in 2016, he said the operation followed "conventional grazing, pretty standard for this area." Under that approach, cattle had continuous access to the same areas. This could lead to overgrazing, particularly where the grass was most attractive to the animals, while other parts of the pasture received less attention.The Smileys have since introduced a virtual fencing system called Vence to manage cattle movements. The technology uses satellite connections and GPS-enabled collars, allowing ranchers to control where their animals graze without building physical fences. Using a computer or tablet, the couple can draw boundaries on a digital map. These boundaries create grazing areas, known as cells, which can be made larger or smaller depending on the management plan.When cattle approach a virtual boundary, their collars produce a sound warning. If they continue towards the boundary, the collars deliver a mild electrical signal. The animals learn to respond to the warnings and remain within the assigned area. The Smileys plan their grazing schedules in advance. They decide how long cattle should stay in each cell by considering the amount of available grass and the size of the herd. Once the grazing period ends, they move the virtual boundary to guide the cattle into another area.Recovery of the native grasslandsOne of the biggest benefits of rotational grazing is the time it gives grass to recover. Allowing plants to grow again between grazing periods helps improve their health and strengthens their roots. Caden Smiley told the Tri-State Neighbor that he had seen a clear difference since changing the way the ranch operates. "It’s been pretty dramatic, the changes in the grass... Just by giving that rest... the plant community is just so much healthier."Under traditional grazing methods, cattle can repeatedly eat the new growth before plants have enough time to recover. This forces plants to use stored energy in their roots to produce more growth. Over time, repeated grazing can weaken the roots and damage the plants. Rotational grazing helps prevent this problem. Cattle remain in one grazing cell only long enough to feed before being moved to another area. The land then gets a longer period to recover.During this time, plants can grow new leaves, absorb sunlight and rebuild their root systems. Stronger roots help hold soil together, improve water absorption and allow the ground to retain more moisture. This is particularly important around Kadoka, which lies near the Badlands in a semi-arid region. Rainfall and soil moisture are limited, so keeping grasslands healthy is important for the long-term productivity of the ranch. Giving native plants enough time to recover also helps maintain the natural vegetation that supports wildlife across the region.Return of varied wildlife populationsThe improvements to the grasslands have also benefited wildlife. Jori Smiley told the Tri-State Neighbor that healthier pastures have brought greater variety in both plant life and animal populations. Rotational grazing creates different types of vegetation across the ranch. Some areas are being grazed, while others are recovering and developing taller grass. This creates a mixture of habitats that offers wildlife different sources of food and shelter.The Smileys have noticed a clear increase in wildlife, particularly birds. Caden said different types of grassland birds are now nesting and thriving in areas where the grass has been allowed to grow taller. This is important because many grassland bird populations across the Great Plains have been declining. These birds depend on healthy native grasslands for nesting, feeding and protection.The changes have also benefited larger animals. Mule deer and pronghorn antelope are making greater use of the pastures, where they can find different types of plants to eat and areas of taller grass for shelter. The mixture of grazing and recovering land provides more varied conditions for wildlife. Taller grass can offer protection for young animals, while different plants provide food throughout the year. The increased presence of birds and larger mammals suggests that the ranch's changing grazing practices are benefiting more than livestock. The couple's approach is helping support agricultural production while improving conditions for native wildlife.Management over manual labourThe Smileys have also seen major changes in the amount of time and physical work needed to manage their ranch. Traditional rotational grazing often requires ranchers to build and maintain several fences. This can involve installing electric wires or barbed wire, repairing damaged sections and moving fences whenever cattle need access to another pasture. These jobs can take considerable time and money, particularly on large ranches with uneven or difficult terrain. Virtual fencing has reduced much of this work at Smiley Ranch. Instead of spending hours building and repairing physical barriers, Caden can manage cattle movements through the Vence system. He told the Tri-State Neighbor that the time saved has made a major difference to his daily routine. "We spend about five minutes a morning moving cattle and analyzing our pastures." Rather than working constantly along conventional fence lines, the couple can now spend more time reviewing pasture conditions and planning grazing schedules. Digital maps allow them to check where cattle are grazing, estimate how much grass is available and decide when animals should move to another section.The technology also gives them more flexibility when managing large pastures. They can change grazing boundaries without having to build new fences, which is particularly useful in West River South Dakota, where large areas may have limited access to water. The system does not remove every task involved in running the ranch. Water supplies and other parts of the livestock operation still need attention. However, it has reduced the physical work involved in moving cattle between grazing areas. The Smileys' experience since 2016 shows how satellite technology can support traditional land management practices. By combining virtual fencing with rotational grazing, the family has been able to give grasslands more time to recover, reduce daily fencing work and improve habitat for wildlife. Their approach brings together modern technology and established grazing methods, allowing the family to continue ranching while working to maintain healthier grasslands for the future.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI is still weighing on streamers at Twitch’s biggest event of the year
articles.summary: Months after Twitch stirred backlash for allowing Amazon to train AI models on streamers’ content unless they opt out, some TwitchCon attendees remain critics of the technology.
articles.body: SAN DIEGO — “Tone deaf.” “Bland and boring.” “stupid.” Those were some of the reactions from TwitchCon attendees who encountered a surprisingly prominent presence on the expo floor at the streaming platform’s annual convention: OpenAI. The company behind ChatGPT had set up shop to promote its Codex coding tool through a hackathon at the event, which brings together Twitch personalities, their fans and industry experts to discuss the future of streaming. But the booth drew criticism from some attendees who remain uneasy about AI’s growing influence over their creative work. “No one wanted this, and we made that clear,” one Twitch user wrote on X over the weekend, sharing a link to a forum for the community to call on Twitch to end its partnership with AI companies. The negative response from some toward OpenAI’s activation came despite AI being largely absent from TwitchCon’s official programming. The technology remains a divisive issue among streamers, with some eager to experiment with new tools and others concerned about the implications for human creativity and jobs. Just a few months ago, Twitch stoked outrage from its user base when it publicly introduced an option that would allow streamers to opt out of having their content used to train AI models owned by its parent company, Amazon. Streamers who criticized the move said they never consented to their content being scraped in the first place, and that the feature should’ve been opt-in instead of opt-out. But at the San Diego convention this weekend, some streamers said they feel AI tools — such as speech-to-text, auto-captioning and clipping — could be helpful as long as they’re not used to generate content and replace human creativity. “I do think it’s useful in a sense of accessibility for people who may not be able to do certain things,” said TwitchCon attendee Chloe Van Ryn, 31, from Arizona. “I think it could be good for moderator tools or pinpointing new users or things like that, if AI could track that. But I think if it was anything within a creative sense, I really don’t know if it’s a good place for Twitch.” Van Ryn said she’s suspicious about Twitch’s approach to its streamers’ content after it introduced its controversial opt-out toggle. She said she wouldn’t be comfortable with her own content being fed into AI models. “It’s like the same as [when AI companies are] taking books and scanning them and then just completely destroying them,” Van Ryn said. “I think it’s definitely something like you have to know you’re opting into it. And I think it’s really important that your people, your community, know whether you’re opting in or not.” Others expressed more staunchly anti-AI views. “I’m not a fan of AI. If you are so desperate and trying to cling to it, there are creators who use AI. Go to those people,” said Rummeko, who asked to be identified by his Twitch username. “But I think to make [AI content scraping] widespread for all, and we all have to go in several layers deep to turn it off, I think that’s an entirely wrong and disrespectful way to go about it.” When asked about streamers’ concerns surrounding their content being potentially fed to Amazon’s AI models, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told NBC News that being automatically opted in doesn’t mean a user’s data has already been scraped. He said the toggle is intended to be a preventive measure in case Amazon does have plans to train its AI on Twitch content. “We in fact said, ‘Well, look, if Amazon wants to use this data — that doesn’t mean they are, I am not involved in [what Amazon is doing] — we want our creators to have the ability to opt out,’” Clancy said. “And that way, wherever this is going, our creators are able to express their wishes.” It’s unclear whether Amazon has already used content from Twitch to train its models. Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In an interview at TwitchCon, Twitch’s Chief Product Officer Mike Minton declined to comment the matter, citing lawsuits from streamers filed in response to the controversy. “In terms of what’s happened in the past, due to ongoing litigation, I have nothing to say,” Minton said. Clancy and Minton said that most other services don’t give users the option to opt out of their content being used for AI training — and that by making that option available, Twitch put a spotlight on itself despite the issue not being unique to the company. “There’s a trade-off there, and we felt it was important to offer the option,” Minton said. “That obviously drove a conversation, drove a moment around creators’ concerns and fears around generative AI. And unfortunately, in those moments, a lot of the nuance gets lost.”
